verifications.claim: Roughly three dozen countries, primarily in the Americas, grant unconditional birthright citizenship (jus soli) to nearly everyone born on their soil.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Roughly three dozen countries across the globe have unconditional birthright citizenship... Most of them are in the western hemisphere, ranging from Canada to Chile.'; R2: 'about three dozen countries provide for unrestricted citizenship at birth... almost every country in the Americas has unrestricted birthright citizenship.'; R3: 'About three dozen countries have unrestricted birthright citizenship... nearly every country in Central and South America.'; R4: 'Only about three dozen countries around the world, mostly in the Western Hemisphere, offer automatic birthright citizenship.'
verifications.reasoning: All references directly state or closely match 'roughly/about three dozen' countries with unconditional/unrestricted/automatic birthright citizenship, primarily/mostly/almost every in the Americas/Western Hemisphere.

verifications.claim: The U.S. grants unconditional birthright citizenship (jus soli) to nearly everyone born on its soil.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R2: 'The U.S. is one of about three dozen countries that provide for unrestricted citizenship at birth.'; R3: 'The U.S. is joined by neighbors Canada and Mexico, along with nearly every country...'; R4: 'birthright citizenship became part of the Constitution in 1868... constitutionally enshrined practice'; R1: context of U.S. policy discussion with 'unconditional birthright citizenship' in other countries.
verifications.reasoning: References explicitly or by strong context confirm U.S. has unconditional/unrestricted birthright citizenship.

verifications.claim: Unconditional birthright citizenship (jus soli) is rare in Europe and Asia.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Most countries in Europe, by contrast,' (implying rare); R3: 'No country in Europe or East Asia, for example, has a similar policy.'; R4: 'mostly in the Western Hemisphere'; R2: many Eastern Hemisphere changed away from it.

verifications.claim: Citizenship in Europe and Asia is usually based on parentage (jus sanguinis).
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'Most countries in Europe... confer citizenship based on parents’ lineage'; R2: 'changed laws from citizenship by place of birth to citizenship by parental nationality'; R4: 'Many countries offer citizenship instead via jus sanguinis, or "right of blood."'
verifications.reasoning: References directly state most/usually in Europe and others use parentage/lineage/jus sanguinis.
